newsitem.title: USA: Jewish leader says Swiss conflict may be near end.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader says Swiss conflict may be near end.

text.p: The two-year long controversy over Swiss handling of Jewish and Nazi assets during the Second World War could be near an end, a Jewish leader active in the fight said on Thursday.

Elan Steinberg, executive director of the World Jewish Congress, said in an interview that ending the controversy depended on how Swiss authorities followed through on commitments made in the last few weeks.
But Steinberg cautioned that an essential problem remained for the Swiss even if the controversy with world Jewry ended.
"They have still to come to terms with the moral aspects of the questions over how they acted in the war and in the years afterwards," he said.

He added, "The mechanical elements for closure are in place. In many respects, the Swiss bankers and authorities have come to agree on the mechanism and procedures we have struggled for in the last two years."

But he said no matter what financial restitution was made it had "to be accompanied by moral restitution and here there are troubling questions such as Swiss attacks on a recent U.S. government report which examined Nazi Germany's links to neutral countries."

The report, prepared under the direction of State Department Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat, said Swiss financial dealings with Germany may have prolonged the war. It also criticised six other nations, including the United States. But Steinberg said, "Only the Swiss government has seen fit to attack this remarkable study."

In the last few weeks, the Swiss have agreed to quickly begin payments for Holocaust survivors, especially in Eastern Europe, and to quickly get an independent panel in place to arbitrate claims from heirs to dormant Jewish accounts still in Swiss banks more than 50 years after the war.

Another Jewish leader close to the negotiations said a Swiss-Jewish board will meet in about two weeks and the first item on its agenda is to start authorising the payment of millions of dollars to Holocaust survivors in about two weeks.
He said the first authorisation would be $60 million to aid about 60,000 Holocaust survivors in Eastern Europe. They would each receive about 1,000.

The money would come from a special $200 million humanitarian fund for Holocaust victims established by Swiss banks earlier in the year and administered by a board of Swiss and Jewish representatives.
Jewish groups have pressed hard for the fund, saying time was running out to help Holocaust survivors whose average age now is about 80.
Switzerland on Wednesday announced that it was setting up a special independent panel to resolve claims by survivors to dormant accounts still in Swiss banks.

The whole issue of Swiss action during the Second World War became a controversy when the WJC asked the Swiss Bankers Association for a detailed listing of dormant accounts and the association refused.
That led to a search of the U.S. National Archives which uncovered extensive business links between neutral Switzerland and Nazi Germany, including Swiss laundering of looted Nazi gold.

Now a Swiss historians' commission is looking into the questions of Swiss-Nazi relations and is expected to produce an interim report on Swiss gold transactions with Germany by the end of the year, the WJC's Steinberg said.
Early next year, the commission will also produce an interim report on Swiss refugee policy with regard to Jews.
Switzerland turned away thousands of Jews during the war and put thousands of others in forced labour camps with their upkeep being paid for by Jewish groups.
